analysis.one_liner: Limits religious-exemption claims so they cannot override civil rights, wage, or health coverage laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 33 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 (RFRA), the law that lets people challenge rules that burden their religious practice. It would carve out civil rights protections, wage and benefit requirements, child labor protections, and health care access and coverage rules from RFRA, so a religious objection could not be used to escape those requirements. It would also bar RFRA defenses in lawsuits between private parties and stop RFRA from being used to deny goods or services the government has agreed to provide.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants protected by wage, benefit, leave, and collective-activity laws; women and LGBTQ people who would otherwise face religious-exemption refusals of contraceptive coverage or equal services; children protected by child labor and anti-abuse laws; and people with disabilities covered by the Americans with Disabilities Act. All of them would gain a guarantee that a religious exemption claimed by an employer, business, or government contractor cannot override these protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, patients, and people facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Bars RFRA from overriding protections against discrimination and for equal opportunity, naming the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Violence Against Women Act, and HUD's equal access housing rule.
Bars RFRA from overriding requirements that employers pay wages and provide benefits including leave, and from overriding standards protecting collective activity in the workplace.
Bars RFRA from overriding protections against child labor, child abuse, and child exploitation.

Bars RFRA from being used to deny access to, information about, or coverage for any health care item or service, which under current law has been the basis for employers and religious institutions seeking exemptions from contraceptive coverage requirements.

Limits RFRA claims to cases where the government is a party, so a person could no longer raise a religious-freedom defense against another private party, for example in a private discrimination lawsuit.

Prevents RFRA from being used to deny a beneficiary goods or services the government has contracted, granted, or agreed to provide, or to deny anyone full and equal enjoyment of a government-provided benefit or accommodation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and religiously affiliated institutions that currently invoke RFRA to seek exemptions from wage, benefit, health coverage, or nondiscrimination requirements would have to comply with those laws like everyone else. That means paying for required health coverage, following civil rights rules, and dropping religious-exemption litigation strategies. Religious objectors would lose a legal shield they currently hold in exactly these areas.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows RFRA, the legal shield courts have used to accommodate religious objectors since the Supreme Court's 2014 Hobby Lobby decision. People and institutions with sincere religious objections to providing or covering health care would lose that defense in the specific areas the bill covers, and a good-faith objection is that conscience should still matter in these disputes.

The carve-outs are broad: the health care exemption covers 'any health care item or service,' not only contraception, and courts would be barred from weighing any religious burden in these areas, even cases where the claimed harm to a third party is debatable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core purpose is to stop a religious exemption claimed by one party from shifting real costs onto another: an employee losing mandated benefits, a beneficiary losing a government-funded service, a person being refused equal treatment. The cost falls on religious objectors in those same areas, who would lose a litigation defense the Supreme Court has expanded. That is a real loss for them, but the bill leaves RFRA in place everywhere else, so the trade is narrower than critics' blanket objections suggest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Kamala Harris introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, with an original list of 24 Senate cosponsors including Senators Baldwin, Booker, Brown, Durbin, Klobuchar, Murray, Warren, and Wyden.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The cosponsor list grew to 33 senators, 32 Democrats and 1 independent, but no further action of any kind was taken after the referral.
The bill sat in committee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and religiously affiliated institutions that use RFRA to seek exemptions from health coverage, wage, and nondiscrimination rules are better off, because that defense remains fully intact. Workers, women, and LGBTQ people gained nothing, since the protections the bill would have secured against exemptions were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and religious institutions still claiming RFRA exemptions

for.name: Kamala Harris
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Do No Harm Act in the Senate on February 28, 2019.

for.name: 33 Senate cosponsors (32 Democrats and 1 independent)
for.role: Cosponsors, including Baldwin, Booker, Brown, Durbin, Klobuchar, Murray, Warren, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Lindsey Graham, R-SC)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the action history shows no committee activity after the February 2019 referral.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Religious-liberty advocacy groups
against.role: Outside organizations defending broad RFRA exemptions
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Do No Harm Act, arguing it would strip religious objectors of protections affirmed in cases like Hobby Lobby.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all 33 cosponsors were Democrats or an independent, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Religiously affiliated employers and institutions (hospitals, schools, charities)
industries.note: These institutions have used RFRA to seek exemptions from contraceptive-coverage mandates and employment nondiscrimination rules. The bill would remove that shield, requiring them to follow the same wage, benefit, and civil rights rules as other employers, which is exactly what their workers and patients would gain.

industries.industry: Businesses claiming religious objections (the Hobby Lobby model)
industries.note: For-profit owners have used RFRA to win exemptions from laws covering their employees, such as the contraceptive coverage mandate. The bill would end that strategy for civil rights, wage, benefit, and health care rules, shifting the cost of those requirements back onto the business.

industries.industry: Government contractors and grantees refusing services on religious grounds
industries.note: Organizations receiving government contracts or grants could no longer invoke RFRA to withhold contracted goods or services from beneficiaries, so beneficiaries would get the services taxpayers funded.
